summary: Barry County, MO: steel tower completed May 1936 (99 ft 9 in to the cabin) on the Sugar Camp byway; Forest Service lists it as a picnic stop where climbing is not allowed.

facts.design: Steel tower, 99 feet 9 inches high to the steel cabin (1936 report)
facts.agency: Mark Twain National Forest (USDA Forest Service); Kings River Ranger District in 1936

staffing.status: Two men named in June 1936 as in charge of a look-out tower between Eagle Rock and Seligman (tower not named)

access.note: Picnic stop at the tower on the Sugar Camp National Forest Scenic Byway; the Forest Service says climbing the tower is not allowed

visit.trail_note: Reached by gravel forest road: Forest Road 1004 from Forest Road 197; the byway includes about 8 miles of gravel road

events.note: Newspaper notice: a 100-foot fire tower to be built a short distance east of Seligman by forestry service workers

Steel tower completed May 27, 1936, eight days after work began, by a crew of 15 under Foreman Hopkins; 99 feet 9 inches to the cabin. The Forest Service later credits the Civilian Conservation Corps with building it in the 1930s
Varner Ball and Orville Hodges named in June 1936 as in charge of 'the look-out tower between Eagle Rock and Seligman'; the item does not name the tower

evidence.supports: Dec 1935 notice: 100-foot fire tower to be built east of Seligman by forestry service workers
evidence.quote: A 100-foot fire tower will be constructed a short distance east of Seligman by forestry service workers

evidence.supports: Cassville Republican (June 4, 1936) names the steel tower the Sugar Camp Tower; 99 feet 9 inches to the steel cabin
evidence.quote: The Sugar Camp Tower, located in SE 1-4 SE 1-4, Section 15, Township 21, Range 27, of the Kings River Ranger District, is a steel structure 99 feet 9 inches high to the steel cabin.

evidence.supports: Tower completed May 27, 1936 by a crew of 15 under Foreman Hopkins, eight days after construction began
evidence.quote: This tower was completed May 27 by a crew of 15 men under the supervision of Foreman Hopkins, just eight days after construction was begun.

evidence.supports: Two men in charge of the look-out tower between Eagle Rock and Seligman, June 1936
evidence.quote: Varner Ball and Orville Hodges are in charge of the look-out tower between Eagle Rock and Seligman.

evidence.supports: Forest Service attributes the tower's construction to the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s
evidence.quote: This lookout tower was built by the Civilian Conservation Corp in the 1930s.

evidence.supports: Climbing the tower is not allowed
evidence.quote: Climbing the tower is not allowed.
This is a beautiful site to stop and have a picnic.

evidence.supports: Byway includes about 8 miles of gravel road
evidence.quote: a nice 8-mile section of national forest scenic byway on maintained gravel-road

evidence.supports: Forest Road 1004 leads to the tower from Forest Road 197
evidence.quote: Shortly after joining Forest Road 197, take a right at Forest Road 1004 to see Sugar Camp Fire Tower

evidence.supports: Byway is 28 miles, including about 8 miles of gravel road
evidence.quote: Travel on this 28-mile drive, which combines 20 miles of paved highway and a nice 8-mile section of national forest scenic byway on maintained gravel-road.

evidence.supports: Gravel section turns off Highway 112 shortly after Roaring River State Park
evidence.quote: Look for a Sugar Camp National Forest Scenic Byway sign pointing out the turn to this portion of the byway on Highway 112, shortly after passing through Roaring River State Park.

corrections.why: The 1936 report gives 99 feet 9 inches to the steel cabin, which is 30.4 m. The brief's 30.5 m rounds up from 100 feet.

sources.title: Sugar Camp National Forest Scenic Byway
sources.publisher: Mark Twain National Forest (USDA Forest Service)

notes_for_editor: Standing and public picnic access rest on the Forest Service byway page, which is undated and uses present tense. The 1935 notice places the planned tower 'a short distance east of Seligman', but the 1936 report and the Forest Service page place Sugar Camp near Roaring River, and the Forest Lookouts page groups the two as one tower; not reconciled. Builder attribution differs (forestry service workers and a 15-man crew in 1936 vs CCC per the Forest Service); both kept in the story. The June 1936 item naming Ball and Hodges does not name the tower, so the staffed event is hedged. No fire or rental information found in readable sources. Facebook group posts were not used.
